Outlier Detection > Basic Concept > Motivation 
5
❑ Outlier (a.k.a. anomaly)
▪ “An observation which deviates so much from other observations as to arouse suspicions that 
it was generated by a different mechanism”
▪ Outlier detection (a.k.a. anomaly detection)
• The process of finding the data objects with behaviors that are very different from expectation 
Image: http://wallpaperswide.com/cats_and_owl-wallpapers.html → regenerated as Ghibli style by ChatGPT

7
❑ Applications of outlier detection
▪ Suspicious credit card transactions
• Most transactions are normal and only very few are abnormal
• e.g., abnormal transactions ([$1K, 1:00PM, Seoul], [$5K, 1:05PM, New York])
▪ Medical care
▪ Public safety and security
▪ Industry damage detection
▪ Sensor and video network surveillance
▪ National security
▪ System intrusion detection

Outlier Detection > Basic Concept > Comparison
14
❑ Pattern Mining vs. Outlier detection
▪ Common pattern vs. Unique pattern
▪ e.g., items bought together vs. items rarely bought
❑ Clustering vs. Outlier detection
▪ Sets of similar objects vs. isolated objects
▪ e.g., customers spending $1K or $10K vs. a customer spending $1B
▪ They are very relevant tasks (e.g., DBSCAN)
❑ Classification vs. Outlier detection
▪ Existing classes vs. Novel classes (novelty detection or one-class classification)
▪ e.g., dog or cat? vs. bird in dogs and cats? 
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Basic Concept > Comparison
15
❑ Similar concepts to outliers
▪ Noise
• A random error or variance in a measured variable, and thus is not interesting in data analysis
• e.g., a random bigger lunch one day or one more cup of coffee than usual
▪ Novelty
• A novel observation that has not been previously encountered but might be anticipated to recur
• e.g., new topics and trends while monitoring social media where new content is incoming
‒ Once new topics are confirmed, they are usually incorporated into the model of normal behavior so that follow-up 
instances are not treated as a novelty anymore
▪ Out-of-distribution (OOD)
• Data objects that come from a different distribution than the distribution used to train a model
‒ e.g., a model is trained on images of dogs to detect dog breeds but receives an image of a cat
• OOD detection is to ensure that models do not make predictions on data they were not designed to handle
▪ No clear boundary exists, but in general, OOD > Novelty > Outlier > Noise
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Basic Concept > Types
16
❑ Global outliers (or point outlier)
▪ A data object is a global outlier if it deviates significantly from the rest of the data set
▪ e.g., “It is 50°C today” – an outlier in Korea
Price
Attribute 2
Time
Attribute 1
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
❑ Contextual outliers (or conditional outlier)
▪ A data object is a contextual outlier if it deviates significantly with respect to a specific context 
of the object in the data set
▪ e.g.,: “It is 35°C today” – outlier in spring in Korea, but may not in summer in Korea

Outlier Detection > Basic Concept > Types
18
❑ Collective outliers
▪ A subset of data objects forms a collective outlier if the objects as a whole deviate significantly 
from the entire data set, while the individual data objects may not be outliers 
▪ e.g., “It has been 35°C for the whole month” – outlier even in summer in Korea

Outlier Detection > Basic Concept > Challenges
19
❑ Lack of labels
▪ Outliers are rare by nature, so it is difficult to get sufficient labeled data
❑ Modeling normal objects and outliers
▪ The border between data normality and abnormality (outliers) is often not clear-cut 
❑ Application-specific outliers
▪ The relationship among objects highly depends on applications
❑ Handling noise
▪ Noise often unavoidably exists in data collected in many applications 
▪ Low data quality and the presence of noise bring a huge challenge to outlier detection 
❑ Interpretability
▪ A user may want to not only detect outliers, but also understand why they are outliers 
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Basic Concept > Approaches
20
❑ Supervision
▪ Supervised methods
• Assumption: normal and abnormal labels are available
• e.g., classification with imbalanced data sets 
‒ Sampling and augmentation are often required to avoid many false positives
▪ Unsupervised or semi-supervised methods
• Assumption: only normal labels are available or assume that normal objects are somewhat “clustered”
• e.g., nearest neighbors, local density, angle, tree

Outlier Detection > Statistical Methods
23
❑ Make assumptions about data normality fitting the given data set
▪ Assume that normal objects in a data set are generated by a statistical model
▪ Estimate the probability of objects and regard objects in the regions of low probability as outliers
❑ Approaches
▪ Parametric method
▪ A nonparametric method 
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Statistical Methods
24
❑ Parametric method
▪ Assumes that the normal data objects are generated by a parametric distribution with a finite 
number of parameters Θ
▪ The probability density function of the parametric distribution f(x|Θ) gives the probability that an 
object is generated by the distribution
• The smaller the probability, the more likely the object is an outlier
▪ Approaches
• Boxplot
• Normal distribution
• Grubb’s test
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Statistical > Parametric
25
❑ Boxplot
▪ A five-number summary
• The smallest nonoutlier value (Min), the lower quartile (Q1), the median (Q2), the upper quartile (Q3), 
and the largest nonoutlier value (Max) 
• The interquartile range (IQR): Q3 − Q1 
• Normal range: the region between Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR
• Outliers: any object outside the normal region
Image: https://www.atlassian.com/data/charts/box-plot-complete-guide
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Statistical > Parametric

❑ Z-score
▪ Assumes that data objects are generated from a normal (Gaussian) distribution
▪ Learn the parameters of the normal distribution and identify the points of low probability as outliers

Outlier Detection > Statistical > Parametric

❑ Z-score
▪ Assumes that data objects are generated from a normal (Gaussian) distribution
▪ Learn the parameters of the normal distribution and identify the points of low probability as outliers
▪ Example
• Suppose average temperature values in July in the last 10 years are as follows
‒ 24.0◦C, 28.9◦C, 28.9◦C, 29.0◦C, 29.1◦C, 29.1◦C, 29.2◦C, 29.2◦C, 29.3◦C, and 29.4◦C
• A normal distribution of average temperature is estimated by the mean μ and the standard deviation σ

▪ A statistical test if the suspected outlier significantly deviates from the mean of the normally 
distributed data set
▪ For each object x in a data set, compare its z-score 𝑧 =

Outlier Detection > Statistical Methods
29
❑ A nonparametric method 
▪ Tries to determine the model from the input data without assuming a statistical model
• The number and nature of parameters are flexible and not fixed in advance
▪ Require more data and results can be more difficult to interpret compared to parametric methods
▪ Approaches
• Histogram
• Kernel density estimation
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Statistical > Non-Parametric
30
❑ Histogram
▪ Construct a histogram using the input data set
▪ If a new object falls in one of the histogram’s bins, the object is normal, and otherwise, an outlier
▪ Use the histogram to assign an outlier score to an object
• E.g., the inverse of the volume of the bin in which the object falls
‒ Amount: $7500 → score = 1/(100-(60+20+10+6.7+3.1))%=1/0.2%=500
‒ Amount: $385 → score = 1/60% = 1.67
▪ Drawbacks: hard to choose an appropriate bin size
Image: wikipedia
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Statistical > Non-Parametric
31
❑ Kernel density estimation (KDE)
▪ Estimate the probability density function (PDF) of a dataset X with a kernel function
▪ Given a point xi in X, the kernel density estimator computes how likely x i is drawn from X
• The density at xi = ሚ𝑓 𝑥𝑖 = 1
𝑚 σ𝑗=1..𝑚𝐾ℎ(|𝑥𝑖 − 𝑘𝑐𝑗|)
‒ 𝐾ℎ() is a kernel function (e.g., Gaussian function) with a bandwidth ℎ and 𝑘𝑐𝑗 is a kernel center
• Typically, each data point in a dataset is used as a kernel center
▪ A data point with a low density can be considered as an outlier
Image: wikipedia

Outlier Detection > Proximity-based Methods 
34
❑ Basic idea
▪ Proximity: closeness; the state of being near
▪ Intuition: objects that are far from others can be regarded as outliers
▪ Assumption: the proximity of an outlier object to its nearest neighbors significantly deviates 
from the proximity of most other objects to their nearest neighbors

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Proximity-based Methods 
35
❑ Two types of proximity-based methods
▪ Distance-based
• An object is identified as an outlier if it is relatively far from its neighboring objects (e.g., kNN)
▪ Density-based
• An object is identified as an outlier if its density is relatively much lower than that of its neighboring objects

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Proximity > Distance-based
36
❑ kNN as a binary output inlier/outlier
▪ Let R (R ≥ 0) be a distance threshold and F (0 < F ≤ 1) be a fraction threshold
▪ Given a data set D, an object o is a DB(R,F)-outlier if 𝑜′ 𝑑 𝑜, 𝑜′ ≤ 𝑅, 𝑜≠𝑜′
|𝐷| < 𝐹
• i.e., 𝑜′ 𝑑 𝑜, 𝑜′ ≤ 𝑅, 𝑜≠𝑜′ < K (= |D| × F)
• Excluding the base object itself when counting neighbors

COSE471: Data Science

Outlier Detection > Proximity > Distance-based
37
❑ A naive nested-loop algorithm for distance-based outlier detection
▪ Definition: DB(R,F)-outlier = 𝑜′ 𝑑 𝑜, 𝑜′ ≤ 𝑹 , 𝑜≠𝑜′ < 𝐊 (= |D| × F)
▪ Input: a dataset D, a distance threshold R, a neighbor count threshold K
▪ For i = 1 to |D| do
• Set neighbor count of oi, counti = 0;
• For j = 1 to |D| do 
‒ if (i ≠ j, d(oi, oj) ≤ R) then counti = counti + 1;
• If counti < K then output oi as an outlier;
▪ Complexity with no explicit index used: O(|D|2)
▪ An implementation trick
• If an object has K neighbors (i.e., counti = K), stop counting further
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Proximity > Distance-based
38
❑ Strategies to accelerate scalability 
▪ Try to minimize pairwise distance calculation for all objects in a data set
▪ Cell-based, index-based, sampling-based, …
❑ Cell-based strategy – overview
▪ Find a small region (i.e., a cell) in which objects are guaranteed to be neighbors (i.e., 𝑑 𝑜, 𝑜′ ≤ 𝑅)
▪ Identify and prune the inlier-guaranteed regions and the outlier-guaranteed regions
▪ Investigate only the objects in the remaining regions

Outlier Detection > Proximity > Distance-based
39
❑ Cell-based strategy – definitions
▪ Assuming that 𝑑 ∙,∙  is the Euclidean distance (i.e., 𝑑(𝑜𝑖, 𝑜𝑗) =
2
|𝑜𝑖1 − 𝑜𝑗1|2 + |𝑜𝑖2 − 𝑜𝑗2|2 + ⋯ + |𝑜𝑖𝑘 − 𝑜𝑗𝑘|2)
▪ A cell: a hypercube partitioning the entire data space
• The diagonal length of a cell in d-dimensional space is at most 𝑅 (i.e., the maximum distance inside the cell)
‒ The length of each side of a cell becomes 𝑅/ 𝑑 (e.g., 𝑅 for 1-dimensional, 𝑅/ 2 for 2-dimensional, …)
• Any two objects in the cell are guaranteed to be neighbors
▪ Neighboring cells: the two cells whose centers are less than 2 ×R far away
‒ i.e., cells C and C’ are neighbors if d(C, C’) < 2R
‒ If two cells are neighboring cells, two objects respectively in the two cells might be neighbors
‒ If two cells are not neighboring cells, two objects respectively in the two cells can never be neighbors

Outlier Detection > Proximity > Distance-based
41
❑ Cell-based strategy – cell-level detection
▪ Inlier cell (      )
• All objects in the cell are inliers
• Lower bound on the number of neighbors >= K 
‒ i.e., card(C) - 1 >= K.
▪ Outlier cell (      )
• All objects in the cell are outliers
• Upper bound on the number of neighbors < K 
‒ i.e., card(C) + sum(card(C’) | d(C,C’) < 2R) - 1 < K
▪ Non-determined cell (      )
• Neither inlier cell nor outlier cell
‒ It is not sure if the objects in the cell are all inliers or outliers
• Passed to the object-level detection
K = 3

Outlier Detection > Proximity > Distance-based
43
❑ Advanced topics 
▪ High-dimensional data
• Downward-closure property of neighbors (feat. Downward-closure property of frequent itemsets)
‒ Neighbors in full-dim ⇒  Neighbors in sub-dim
‒ i.e., a set of neighbors in full-dim ⊆  a set of neighbors in sub-dim
• Two-level dimensional filtering
‒ Find outliers and neighbors early in the sub-dimensional space
▪ Multiple outlier detection queries scenario
• Multiple queries – different number of neighbors and distance thresholds
▪ Streaming scenario
• Distribution of data points and queries change over time

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Proximity > Density-based
48
❑ Local outlier factor (LOF)
▪ Define a notion of density with k nearest neighbors (kNN)
▪ Relevant concept used for clustering?
• [Recap] DBSCAN
‒ A density-based notion of cluster as a maximal set of density-connected points
‒ The Eps-neighborhood of a point x: NEps(x) = {p | d(p, x) ≤ Eps}
‒ Core point: in a dense neighborhood (i.e., cluster)
i.e., |NEps(x)| ≥ MinPts
‒ Border point: not a core point, but the neighbor of a core point
i.e., |NEps(x)| < MinPts, but x ∈ NEps(x’) for a core point x’
‒ Outlier/noise: neither a core point nor the neighbor of a core point
• Outlier/noise is defined by static Eps-neighborhood
▪ “Relative” density is considered as local proximity

❑ Local outlier factor (LOF)
▪ Define a notion of density with k nearest neighbors (kNN)
▪ “Relative” density is considered as local proximity
❑ Building blocks for local outlier factor (LOF)
1. k-distance 
2. k-distance neighborhood

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Proximity > Density-based > LOF
51
❑ Local outlier factor (LOF)
▪ Define a notion of density with k nearest neighbors (kNN)
▪ “Relative” density is considered as local proximity
❑ Building blocks for local outlier factor (LOF)
1. k-distance → the distance to find your neighbors 
2. k-distance neighborhood → the area your neighbors reside
3. Reachability distance → relative distance from your neighbors
4. Local reachability density → local density from relative distances from your neighbors
5. Local outlier factor → relative density to your neighbors
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > Proximity > Density-based > LOF
52
❑ Building blocks for local outlier factor (LOF)
▪ k-distance → k-distance neighborhood → Reachability distance → Local reachability density → Local outlier factor
▪ k-distance
• The k-distance 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑘(𝑜) is the distance between o and its k-nearest neighbor 𝑝
• Formerly, 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑘(𝑜) is the distance 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝑜, 𝑝) between o and another object 𝑝 ∈ 𝐷 that satisfies
‒ There are at least k objects 𝑜′∈ 𝐷\{𝑜} such that 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡 𝑜, 𝑜′ ≤ 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡 𝑜, 𝑝 = 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑘 𝑜
‒ There are at most k−1 objects 𝑜′′∈ 𝐷\{𝑜} such that 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡 𝑜, 𝑜′′ < 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡 𝑜, 𝑝 = 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑘 𝑜

▪ Reachability distance
• For o and p, the reachability distance from o to p is 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑘(𝑜) if 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑘 𝑜 > 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝑜, 𝑝); 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡(𝑜, 𝑝) otherwise

❑ Local outlier factor (LOF) of an object o
▪ The average of the ratio of the local reachability density of o and those of k-distance neighborhood of o
𝐿𝑂𝐹𝑘 𝑜 = 1

𝑙𝑟𝑑𝑘 𝑜
❑ Interpretation of LOF
▪ LOF(o) < 1: an object o is in a relatively denser region
▪ LOF(o) > 1: an object o is in a relatively sparser region
Image: wikipedia

Outlier Detection > Proximity > Density-based > LOF

❑ Properties of LOF
▪ For an object deep within a consistent cluster, LOF is close to 1 
• The density of the object is comparable to those of its neighbors 
• The objects inside clusters, whether dense or sparse, can not be outliers
▪ Bounds on LOF with the reachability distance to (indirect) neighbors
• 𝐿𝑂𝐹𝑘 𝑜 =

❑ [Recap] Kernel density estimation (KDE)
▪ A non-parametric method to estimate the probability density function (PDF) of a dataset X
▪ Given a point xi, the kernel density estimator of X computes how likely xi is drawn from X
• The density at xi in X is ሚ𝑓 𝑥𝑖 = 1
𝑚 σ𝑗=1..𝑚𝐾ℎ(|𝑥𝑖 − 𝑘𝑐𝑗|)
▪ Kernel center 𝑘𝑐
• Each kernel center kcj carries a kernel function Kh. 
• dist(kcj, xi) gives the density contribution to xi  by kcj
• Typically all data points
▪ Kernel function 𝐾ℎ(𝑢)
• A non-negative real-valued integrable function satisfying
‒׬−∞
∞
𝐾 𝑢 𝑑𝑢 = 1 and 𝐾 −𝑢 = 𝐾(𝑢) for any 𝑢
• Gaussian kernel function is the most popular one
• h is the bandwidth serving as a smoothing parameter 
Image: wikipedia

❑ Approximate KDE-based local outlier score
▪ Considering all objects as kernel centers is expensive 
• O(N2) for density estimation
▪ Approximate kernel center AKC
• Abstract kernel center (e.g., micro-cluster or cell centroids)
• Sampled kernel center (e.g., randomly sampled from data points)
▪ Local density estimation
• Estimates the density of xi with only the local AKCs

Outlier Detection > High-dimensional Data
74
❑ Challenges
▪ Data subspace
• Since many features (dimensions) are involved, proper interpretation of the outliers is more useful
• Identifying specific subspaces that manifest the outliers helps users understand the meaning of outliers
‒ Using a fixed-distance threshold against all subspaces may not be a good idea
▪ Data sparsity
• The distance between objects becomes heavily dominated by noise as the dimensionality increases
▪ Scalability to dimensionality
• Exhaustive combinatorial exploration of the search space is not scalable

DAIS lab at Korea University

▪ Angle-based

❑ Extend the conventional proximity-based methods
▪ Try to overcome the curse of dimensionality for proximity measures in high-dimensional spaces 
▪ Use alternative measures or construct subspaces and detect outliers there
❑ Dimensionality reduction
▪ Principal component analysis (PCA), matrix factorization, …
❑ Space-filling curve (serialization)
▪ HilOut finds distance-based outliers, but uses the ranks of 
distance instead of the absolute value
• Find the approximate k-nearest neighbors of o, denoted by 
𝑛𝑛1 𝑜 , … , 𝑛𝑛𝑘 𝑜
‒ Space-filling curve is used to get one-dimensional distances
• The outlier score of object o is 𝑤 𝑜 = σ𝑖=1
𝑘 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡 𝑜, 𝑛𝑛𝑖 𝑜
• The top-N scored objects are output as outliers

Outlier Detection > High-dim > Proximity-based

❑ Subspace-based pruning
▪ A distance-based outlier 𝑜 defined by K neighbors in distance of R. i.e.,  𝑜′ dist 𝑜, 𝑜′ ≤ 𝑅 ≤ K
• Assume that Euclidean distance is used
▪ Downward-closure property of neighbors (feat. downward-closure property of frequent itemsets)
• Distance in sub-dim ≤ distance in full-dim => A set of neighbors in full-dim ⊆ a set of neighbors in sub-dim
▪ Find outlier-guaranteed cells and/or neighbor candidates early in the sub-dimensional space
• The optimal number of sub-dimensions depend on the concentration of data over dimensions

Outlier Detection > High-dim > Angle-based
78
❑ Angle-based outlier detection (ABOD)
▪ A direction-focused measure that does not degrade in high-dimensional data
▪ Idea
• An object is abnormal if most other objects are located in similar directions
• An object is normal if many other objects are located in varying directions
Image: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8715-9_27

❑ Angle-based outlier detection (ABOD)
▪ A direction-focused measure that does not deteriorate in high-dimensional data

Outlier Detection > High-dim > Ensemble-based
80
❑ Isolation forest 
▪ Intuition: it is easier to separate an object from the other objects by randomly splitting the space
Image: https://www.precisely.com/blog/data-enrichment/identifying-location-outliers-using-isolation-forest-in-scala-spark

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Outlier Detection > High-dim > Ensemble-based
81
❑ Isolation forest 
▪ Build various trees and check when an object is isolated
▪ Procedure
• Initialize a forest (i.e., an empty set of trees)
• For the number of trees t,
‒ Randomly sample a subset of a data set
‒ Build a tree from the sampled subset with
1) Randomly selected splitting attribute 
2) Randomly selected splitting point
‒ Add a tree to the forest
Image: https://www.actuview.com/media/downloadAttachment/key/756ca07ee/maid/257, https://wiki.datrics.ai/isolation-forest-model
COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
Depth
Outlier Detection > High-dim > Ensemble-based
82
❑ Isolation forest 
▪ Build various trees and check when an object is isolated
▪ Procedure
• Initialize a forest (i.e., an empty set of trees)
• Build a set of trees from the sampled subset
▪ Evaluation
• For an object x, calculate the average path length തℎ 𝑥  of x in 
each tree from the root node to the external node
• Calculate the anomaly score S 𝑥 = 2−തℎ(𝑥)/𝐿 
‒ L: a normalization constant (i.e., an expected path length)
‒ The score → 1: the path length is small (anomaly)
‒ The score → 0.5: the path length is large (normal)
Image: https://wiki.datrics.ai/isolation-forest-model

COSE471: Data Science
DAIS lab at Korea University
❑ Limitation of standard isolation forest 
▪ Ghost area: a region of few objects but lower anomaly scores
• Owing to random splits for one of the fixed random axes (attributes)
▪ Example (darker areas indicate higher anomaly scores)
▪ Extension with hyperplane split
• Rotated isolation forest
• Extended isolation forest

COSE471: Data Science

Outlier Detection > Evaluation
85
❑ By definition, outliers are rare
▪ The ground-truth labels are not always available
❑ When labels are not present 
▪ Qualitative analysis (e.g.,  histograms of anomaly scores)
❑ When labels are present (i.e., binary classification?)
▪ Standard evaluation measures
• ROC (TPR – FPR) curve → AUC score
• Precision-Recall(=TPR) curve → Average Precision score
‒ More useful when the classes are imbalanced (P << N)
‒ FPR (FP/(FP+TN)) in ROC → Precision (TP/(FP+TP))
▪ Top-N evaluation measures (N: # of true outliers)
• Precision@N
• Average Precision@N
Image: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10618-015-0444-8
Ranks of true outliers out of 100 objects
